concept.title: BINARY Data Type ( or higher only)

conbody.p: The BINARY data type stores a variable-length sequence of arbitrary bytes. The difference from STRING is that a STRING is meant to hold text, while a BINARY value can be any byte array, including bytes that are not valid UTF-8.
A BINARY value has no declared length, the same as a STRING value.
There is no BINARY literal. Use CAST(string AS BINARY). To build a value from arbitrary bytes, convert a hexadecimal string with UNHEX() and cast the result:
Unlike Hive, Impala requires the explicit CAST in INSERT ... VALUES, because a STRING is not implicitly converted to BINARY.

BINARY can only be cast to and from STRING. Casts to or from any other type, including CHAR and VARCHAR, are not allowed. Impala does not implicitly convert between BINARY and any other type, so a function that expects a STRING argument does not accept a BINARY value. Cast the value to STRING first, e.g. HEX(CAST(b AS STRING)) to display the bytes in hexadecimal.

ul.li: The comparison operators (=, !=, <, >, <=, >=, IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM) can be used on BINARY values, as well as ORDER BY, DISTINCT, GROUP BY and joins on BINARY columns. The operands must both be BINARY, for example WHERE b = CAST('abc' AS BINARY).

Only a small set of built-in functions accepts BINARY arguments: LENGTH() and BYTES() (both return the size in bytes), CONCAT(), IF(), COALESCE(), ISNULL(), IFNULL(), NVL(), TYPEOF() and MURMUR_HASH(). LENGTH() returns the number of bytes regardless of the UTF8_MODE query option. Other string functions, and LIKE and REGEXP, require a cast to STRING.
COUNT(), COUNT(DISTINCT), MIN() and MAX() are supported. NDV() is not, so cast the column to STRING to estimate the number of distinct values.
COMPUTE STATS does not calculate the number of distinct values of BINARY columns. The other column statistics are computed.

conbody.codeblock: SELECT id, HEX(CAST(b AS STRING)), LENGTH(b) FROM bin_t WHERE b = CAST(UNHEX('00FF00FF') AS BINARY);
conbody.p: BINARY columns cannot be used as partition columns with the PARTITIONED BY (col BINARY) syntax.

ul.li: Text: BINARY values are base64 encoded in text data files. Impala decodes them when reading and encodes them when writing. A value that is not valid base64 is returned as NULL and reported as Error converting column: n to BINARY.

JSON: Before HIVE-21240, Hive wrote binary data to JSON tables as escaped strings, and since then it writes base64 encoded strings by default. Impala therefore needs to know the format. Set the json.binary.format serde property of the table to base64 or rawstring, or set the JSON_BINARY_FORMAT query option for tables where the property is not set. See .
Other HDFS file formats such as Parquet and ORC: BINARY values are stored as the byte arrays of the format, with no base64 encoding.
Kudu: Since , BINARY columns are supported in Kudu tables, and simple predicates on them can be pushed down to Kudu.
Hive Metastore: The column type is stored as binary.

conbody.p: Native UDFs and Java UDFs can use BINARY arguments and return values. For backward compatibility, a Java UDF whose Java type is byte[] or BytesWritable is treated as taking or returning a STRING, unless the argument and return types are specified explicitly as BINARY in the CREATE FUNCTION statement.

Since , BINARY values can be members of STRUCT types and items, keys or values of ARRAY and MAP types. When a complex-typed column is returned directly in the select list, it is displayed in JSON format, and the BINARY values in it are shown base64 encoded, for example {"i":0,"b":"bWVtYmVy"}. Referring to the BINARY member, item, key or value itself returns the raw bytes. See .
